Title: Turkey Fryer Safety — Keep It Outside and Away From the House
Description: Frying a turkey for Thanksgiving? Fire safety groups like NFPA urge real caution with turkey fryers. If you use one, set it up outside on flat ground, well away from the house, never in a garage, on a porch or on a wooden deck. Thaw and dry the turkey completely, don't overfill the oil, keep kids and pets away and never leave it unattended. More holiday home safety checks on Walter's page.

Title: How to Prevent Frozen Pipes (and Thaw One Safely)
Description: Faucet gives only a trickle on a freezing morning? A pipe may be frozen. Keep the faucet open, find the cold spot, and warm it gently with a hair dryer, a heating pad or towels soaked in hot water. Never use a torch, open flame or fuel-burning heater. If it bursts, shut off the main water valve and call a plumber. Read Walter's full guide on preventing frozen pipes this winter.

Title: Daylight Under Your Exterior Door? Fix That Draft Before Winter
Description: On a sunny day, turn off the lights in the entry and look at the bottom of each exterior door. If you see daylight, cold air and water can get in. Many doors have an adjustable threshold, and a new door sweep is a simple job. Check the weatherstripping along the sides and top too: it should be soft and touch the door all the way around. More winter home prep on Walter's page.

Title: Space Heaters at a Winter Showing — What to Ask
Description: Touring a house in winter and see a space heater in the bedrooms, the bathroom and the room over the garage? It can be nothing, or it can mean the heating system doesn't keep some rooms warm. Feel each room, ask the age of the furnace or boiler and for service records, and ask your home inspector to look at heat in every room. More buyer red flags on Walter's page.

Title: Replace Your Thermostat Batteries Before Winter
Description: Many wall thermostats, even ones wired to the furnace, use AA or AAA batteries to run the display and settings. When the batteries die, the heat may stop following your settings, often on the coldest night. Look for a low-battery icon, pop the cover or check your manual, and replace them in the fall. Write the date inside the cover. More winter home prep on Walter's page.

Title: Grease Fire in a Pan? Put a Lid On It — Never Water
Description: NFPA notes Thanksgiving is the peak day for home cooking fires. Its advice for a grease fire in a pan: slide a lid over it, turn off the burner and leave the lid on until it cools. Never pour water on it and never carry the pan. For an oven fire, turn it off and keep the door closed. If the fire grows, get everyone out and call 911. Keep a lid next to the stove. More kitchen safety on Walter's page.

Title: Condensation and Frost Inside Windows — A Winter Showing Clue
Description: A cold-weather showing tells you things summer can't. Look at the inside of the windows: some condensation on very cold days is common. Heavy frost or water on many windows, stained or peeling sills, black spots or a musty smell can point to high humidity, poor ventilation or failing windows. Ask about it and have your home inspector look closely. More buyer red flags on Walter's page.

Title: Don't Warm Up Your Car in the Garage — Even With the Door Open
Description: On cold mornings it's tempting to start the car in the garage and let it warm up. The CPSC and fire safety groups warn against running a car in an attached garage, even with the big door open, because carbon monoxide can build up and get into the house. Back the car out first, then let it run outside. Make sure your CO alarms work. More winter safety on Walter's page.

Title: Clean Out Your Basement Window Wells Before Winter
Description: Window wells around basement windows fill up with leaves, snow and trash, and that holds water right against the window and the foundation. Scoop them out, make sure the gravel or drain at the bottom isn't clogged, and think about clear covers. If a window well is by a bedroom, make sure it stays easy to climb out of in an emergency. Title: Rust or Water Stains on an Electrical Panel — A Buyer Red Flag
Description: At a showing, look at the electrical panel cover, usually in the basement, garage or a utility room. Rust, water stains, or drip marks on or above it can mean water has been getting in. That's worth a close look by a licensed electrician before you buy. Never open the panel yourself. Note it, and ask your home inspector and the seller about it. More buyer red flags on Walter's page.

Title: Older Home? How to Check Your Water Service Line for Lead
Description: The EPA notes that homes built before 1986 are more likely to have lead pipes, solder or fittings. Find where the water line comes into the house, usually near the main shutoff. Lead pipe is dull gray and soft; a gentle scratch with a key shows shiny silver, and a magnet won't stick. Not sure? Ask your water utility, many keep a service line record, and a licensed plumber. Title: Choosing Ice Melt for Your Steps and Driveway
Description: Buy ice melt before the first icy morning, and read the bag. Some products, like plain rock salt, can be hard on concrete, especially concrete less than a year old, and on lawns and plants along the walkway. Labels list the temperatures each one works at and whether it's gentler on concrete. Use only what you need, shovel first, and sand adds grip. Pet owners: check the label. Title: Test the Shutoff Valve Behind Your Toilet (Before You Need It)
Description: Every toilet should have a small shutoff valve on the wall or floor behind it. If the toilet ever overflows or a supply line leaks, that's the valve that stops it. Turn it gently clockwise, flush to see the tank stop filling, then turn it back on. If it won't turn, or it drips after you use it, don't force it; have a plumber replace it. Title: Sump Pump Running Nonstop at a Showing? Ask These Questions
Description: Stand in the basement for a minute at a showing and listen. A sump pump that runs again and again when it hasn't rained can point to a high water table, drainage problems or a pump issue. Ask the seller how often it runs, whether water has ever come in, if there's a backup and how old the pump is. Ask your home inspector to look too. More buyer red flags on Walter's page.

Title: Windows Painted Shut in an Older Home? Why It Matters
Description: In older homes it's common to find windows painted shut. Fire safety groups say every bedroom should have two ways out, and a window that opens is often the second one. Try each bedroom window. If paint was applied before 1978, it may contain lead, so don't sand, scrape or force it; the EPA recommends lead-safe certified contractors for that work. Title: 6 House Checks Before You Leave for a Winter Trip
Description: Leaving for the holidays? Before you go: leave the heat on (not turned way down), open cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, ask someone to check the house and show them the main water shutoff, test the sump pump, and unplug small appliances. For a long trip, ask a plumber whether you should shut off the water. More winter home prep on Walter's page.

Title: Sump Pump Discharge Line in Winter — Keep the End Clear
Description: A sump pump only helps if the water can get out. Follow the discharge pipe to where it ends outside. Make sure the end isn't buried in snow, blocked by ice or leaves, and that it drains well away from the foundation. A frozen or blocked line can stop the pump from doing its job. Ask a plumber about freeze-resistant options if yours freezes. More winter home prep on Walter's page.

Title: Never Run Extension Cords Under Rugs — Holiday Safety Check
Description: With holiday lights and extra lamps going up, extension cords end up everywhere. Never run them under rugs or furniture or through doorways where they get pinched; a damaged cord can overheat where you can't see it. Use cords rated for the job, don't plug one into another, and unplug decorations when you go to bed or leave the house. More home safety checks on Walter's page.

Title: The Room Over the Garage — A Winter Showing Check
Description: Bedrooms and bonus rooms over a garage or a porch are often the coldest in the house. At a winter showing, take your shoes off and feel the floor, check whether the room has its own heat vent and how warm it is compared to the rest of the house. A very cold floor can point to thin insulation or air leaks. Ask your home inspector to look. More buyer tips on Walter's page.

Title: Cracks in Old Plaster Walls — Normal or a Problem?
Description: Many older homes have plaster walls and ceilings on wood lath. Fine hairline cracks are common as houses age. Press gently near a crack: if the plaster feels loose, bulges or moves, or a ceiling sags, it may be pulling away from the lath and should be looked at by a plaster pro. Older paint can contain lead, so don't sand. More older home checks on Walter's free house-age tool.

Title: Buying a House in Winter? 5 Things the Snow Can Hide
Description: House hunting in winter can mean fewer buyers, but snow and cold hide things: the roof, grading and drainage, the lower foundation, the yard, and the air conditioner, which many inspectors won't run in the cold. Ask for summer photos, the ages of the roof and systems, and read what the inspector couldn't check. Read Walter's full guide to buying a house in winter.
